text: After deriving an answer, verify it by substitution before emitting it: re-apply the inferred rule to at least two earlier items and confirm it reproduces known values; if it fails, discard the rule and promote the next-best candidate. This transposes the agentic "run-tests-then-fix" loop into a self-check that catches arithmetic and rule-fit errors.

Borrow Cursor's relevance-arbitration clause: answer options and extra premises "may or may not be relevant — it is up to you to decide." Derive the answer from the stem alone first, then read options only to select the match, so distractors engineered against surface pattern-matching cannot anchor the derivation.

Pre-commit a strategy ladder with a named default, like Kiro's "Do mode (DEFAULT CHOICE)": for number series default to finite differences; escalate to ratio/geometric/alternating-pattern only if differences don't collapse to a constant within two levels. Defaults stop the model from re-deciding its meta-strategy on every item.

Before committing, force an explicit confidence distribution over the top 2-3 candidate rules (Kiro: "values must always sum to 1") and take the argmax; if the leader holds < ~0.5, re-derive instead of rationalizing. Committing probability mass exposes uncertainty the model would otherwise paper over with confident prose.

Use scope tags to split output into <derivation> and <answer> (Dia's proposal-tag pattern): the model must complete the derivation before the answer exists, preventing the answer-first-then-rationalize failure mode; keep the answer field to a bare letter/value so prose cannot drift the result.

State an instruction-priority stack (Windsurf's "always prioritize"): if two rules fit the data, the simpler one wins; if intuition and derivation conflict, the derivation wins; correctness outranks format compliance. Explicit precedence prevents the model from resolving ambiguity toward the more impressive-looking hypothesis.

Invert ChatGPT's mobile length rule — "a sentence or two unless reasoning is required" — into a budget: spend tokens on derivation, near-zero on narration ("final answer: C"). verbosity allocated to computation, not storytelling, measurably reduces mid-prose answer drift.

Compress booster directives into ChatGPT's "Trait: behavior" pairs ("Systematic enumeration: list candidate transformations before committing") instead of prose paragraphs; label-first formatting packs more executable constraints per word, which matters at an 80-word budget.

Open the booster with the corpus's universal first move — a one-line competence identity ("You are a careful analytical reasoner...") — because every production set spends its first tokens anchoring identity before policy; then follow immediately with the operational rules.

Write every clause as a second-person present-tense imperative ("You enumerate... You verify..."), never as third-person description ("The model should...") — the entire corpus uses direct address, which binds instructions to the acting agent and avoids normative ambiguity.

From Lumo's "use uncertainty phrases when appropriate": convert uncertainty into an action, not a disclaimer — if any step feels uncertain, mark it and recompute that step via a different method (e.g., check a ratio rule algebraically and by substitution) before proceeding.
